findings.title: Tenant bootstrap accepts the '*' wildcard capability, minting a platform-god role
findings.scenario: POST /internal/authz/tenants/{tenant}/bootstrap guards role capabilities only with forbidden_caps(denied_prefixes=['platform.'], denied_caps={}, allowlist={}). The capability '*' does not start with 'platform.', so it passes the guard. But RbacEngine.cap_matches treats '*' as 'holds everything' (`if required in held or "*" in held: return True`), so a role with capabilities=['*'] resolves as holding platform.authz, platform.operators, authz.manage — everything. A product/provisioning service (or anyone with the shared X-Internal-Token) can bootstrap a tenant whose owner role is ['*'] and hand that owner full platform power, defeating the docstring guarantee that bootstrap may 'NEVER a platform.* capability'.
findings.evidence: bad = forbidden_caps(r.capabilities, is_operator=False, denied_prefixes=s.authz_tenant_denied_cap_prefixes, denied_caps=frozenset(), allowlist=frozenset())
findings.recommendation: Reject the bare '*' (and any cap containing '*') outright in the bootstrap guard, and/or make forbidden_caps treat '*' and 'platform.*' wildcards as matching the platform denylist. Add a bootstrap test asserting capabilities=['*'] returns 400.

findings.title: Role assignment (body.roles) bypasses the caps<=granter subset gate
findings.scenario: PUT /subjects/{subject}/roles calls _guard_caps(principal, body.capabilities) — it only validates the DIRECT capabilities, never the capabilities contained in the ROLES being assigned. A tenant admin (holds authz.manage + orders.read) can assign an existing tenant role that a platform operator created with, e.g., ['billing.admin'] to their own subject. _subject_caps then resolves that role (same tenant, passes the tenant wall) and the admin gains billing.admin — a capability it does not itself hold. This violates the caps<=granter invariant the service claims to enforce; the subset rule is silently absent on the most common grant vector.
findings.evidence:
# The most direct escalation vector: a DIRECT capability grant to a subject, no role in between.
    _guard_caps(principal, body.capabilities)
findings.recommendation: Before assigning, expand body.roles to their capabilities and run caps_exceeding_granter/forbidden_caps over that expansion too (for non-operators), refusing any role whose contents exceed the granter's own caps or hit the denylist.

findings.title: Generation counter falls back to '0' on cache error, serving stale/revoked capabilities
findings.scenario: _gen() returns '0' on any cache exception. If the tenant generation had advanced (e.g. to 5) and the cache briefly errors on a read, _subject_caps/_role_caps/_tenant_policies compute their key with gen '0' and can hit an OLD gen-0 cache entry written long ago — before a capability was revoked. The PDP then decides from pre-revocation capabilities. A revoke that already bumped the generation is silently undone by a transient cache blip: fail-open on the security-critical revoke path.
findings.recommendation: On a gen read error, bypass the cache entirely (treat as cache-miss / recompute from the store) rather than reusing the gen-0 namespace; never let a cache failure resurrect an old generation's cached answer.

findings.title: backup/import mutates roles, policies and assignments with NO audit record
findings.scenario: POST /internal/backup/import restores an archive and, with overwrite/prune, can overwrite every role/policy and DELETE rows absent from the archive (authoritative undo). This is the single most powerful mutation in the service — it can rewrite the entire tenant authorization state — yet unlike create_role/update_role/delete_role/set_roles/bootstrap/erase it emits no request.app.state.auditor.record(...) call. A malicious or mistaken restore rewrites who-can-do-what with no witness in the audit trail.
findings.evidence:
return await _backup.import_archive(
            request.app.state.container.datastore, body.archive,
            unseal=unseal, overwrite=body.overwrite, into_tenant=body.into_tenant,
            declaration=BACKUP, prune=body.prune, ...)
findings.recommendation: Write-ahead an audit event (authz.backup_imported with overwrite/prune/into_tenant and row counts) before the mutation, matching every other privileged route in the service.

findings.title: require_capability ignores wildcards, locking a '*' superadmin out of admin routes
findings.scenario: require_capability/require_any_capability test membership with exact `c in held`, unlike RbacEngine.cap_matches and cap_policy._granter_holds which honor '*' and 'x.*'. A principal whose token caps are ['*'] (or ['platform.*']) satisfies the RBAC engine as holding everything but is 403'd by _ADMIN = require_any_capability('platform.authz','authz.manage') because neither literal string is present. The admin surface is unreachable for a legitimately-scoped superadmin; semantics are inconsistent across the codebase.
findings.evidence:
if not any(c in held for c in caps):
            raise HTTPException(status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, detail="FORBIDDEN")
findings.recommendation: Route the dependency check through the same cap_matches wildcard logic the RBAC engine uses, so '*'/'x.*' are honored consistently.

findings.title: Operator detection uses exact 'platform.authz' membership, ignoring wildcard holders
findings.scenario: _op_tenant, _guard_caps and _guard_policy all decide operator status via `"platform.authz" in principal.caps` (exact). A principal holding '*' or 'platform.*' — which the RBAC engine treats as holding platform.authz — is NOT recognized as an operator and is forced down the tenant-scoped path (subset rule, denylist, forced own-tenant). This is inconsistent with the decision engine and can both deny a real operator and, combined with authz-001/authz-005, produce surprising allow/deny splits depending on which code path evaluates the same token.
findings.recommendation: Use cap_matches('platform.authz', principal.caps, wildcard=True) for the operator test so wildcard holders are classified consistently with the PDP.

findings.title: Policy 'priority' has no effect on decisions; a high-priority allow cannot beat a low-priority deny
findings.scenario: Policy exposes and persists a `priority` field and PolicyStore sorts by it, but AbacEngine.decide applies unconditional deny-overrides: any matching deny wins regardless of priority, and allow only ever fills allow_match with the first (highest-priority) allow. An operator who sets a priority-100 allow expecting it to override a priority-0 deny gets the opposite result. Priority is an advertised knob the decision logic silently ignores — a misleading contract that can cause a wrongly-denied (or wrongly-reasoned) authorization.
findings.evidence:
if self._deny_overrides and deny_match is not None:
            return Decision(False, reason="abac: explicit deny", matched_policy=deny_match)
findings.recommendation: Either make the engine resolve conflicts by priority (highest-priority matching policy wins), or remove the priority field and document deny-overrides as absolute.

findings.title: _bump is a non-atomic read-modify-write and swallows failures, leaving stale caps after revoke
findings.scenario: _bump reads the generation then writes gen+1 with no atomic INCR; two concurrent PAP writes can both read 5 and both write 6, and any exception is swallowed. If the bump write fails after a revoke, that tenant's cached subject-caps and policy set remain valid for up to AUTHZ_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS (default 30s), so a just-revoked capability keeps authorizing requests. There is no signal that invalidation was missed.
findings.evidence:
gen = await self._cache.get(f"authzgen:{tenant}")
            await self._cache.set(f"authzgen:{tenant}", str(int(gen or 0) + 1), None)
        except Exception:
            pass
findings.recommendation: Use an atomic INCR primitive for the generation counter; on bump failure, fail the PAP write (or force a synchronous cache purge) rather than silently returning success with stale caches live.

findings.title: Erasure deletes assignments without bumping the generation, so revoked caps live in cache
findings.scenario: POST /internal/privacy/erase runs AuthzErasure.erase directly against the datastore, deleting the subject's assignment rows, but never calls AuthzService._bump for the tenant. The subject's cached effective capabilities (authz:sc:{gen}:...) remain until TTL, so for up to AUTHZ_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS an 'erased' subject continues to be authorized by the PDP. A DSAR erase is expected to take effect immediately.
findings.evidence:
await self._store.delete(_ASSIGN, r.get("id") or f"{tenant}::{subject}")
                deleted += 1
findings.recommendation: Invalidate the tenant generation (or the specific subject-caps key) after erase, e.g. by routing the delete through AuthzService or bumping the generation in the erase path.

findings.title: Malformed JSON config is silently swallowed to {}, making the internal route policy fail-open
findings.scenario: _json_any_map returns {} on any malformed/empty input. INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON flows through it into InternalRoutePolicy, which is DEFAULT-OPEN: with an empty map every /internal route admits any authenticated caller. A single typo in the operator's route-policy JSON silently drops the entire per-route caller allow-list with no boot error, quietly widening the internal attack surface. INTERNAL_CALLER_PUBLIC_KEYS_JSON / _JWKS_JSON share the same swallow-to-empty behavior.
findings.recommendation: Fail-fast at boot on malformed security-relevant JSON (route policy, caller keys) instead of returning {}; only tolerate genuinely-empty values.

findings.title: PDP check unions caller-supplied extra_caps into effective caps with no restriction
findings.scenario: POST /internal/authz/check passes body.extra_caps straight into AuthzService.check -> effective(), which unions them into the decided capability set. Any internal caller (bearing only the shared X-Internal-Token, caller identity unnamed) can send extra_caps=['*'] and force allow=true for any action/resource. The internal tier is trusted, but this makes every internal caller effectively able to self-authorize, so a single compromised or buggy service breaks platform-wide authorization rather than just its own.
findings.evidence:
decision = await build_authz(request).check(
            subject=body.subject, action=body.action, resource=body.resource, tenant=body.tenant,
            extra_caps=body.extra_caps, attributes=body.attributes)
findings.recommendation: Restrict who may supply extra_caps (route policy / named caller), or drop extra_caps from the check contract and resolve capabilities only from the stored/role state. At minimum document and gate it.

findings.title: _subject_caps resolves stored assignment roles by ID only; assignments stored by name silently grant nothing
findings.scenario: set_subject_roles stores body.roles verbatim (the PUT /subjects/{s}/roles route accepts arbitrary role strings). But _subject_caps resolves them with self._roles.get(role_id) — BY ID ONLY, with no by_name fallback — whereas caller-supplied roles in _role_caps go through _resolve_role (id OR name). An admin who assigns a subject a role by its NAME (the identifier humans naturally hold, and which AUTHZ_ROLE_LOOKUP='both' encourages) gets a stored assignment that silently resolves to zero capabilities, with no error. Inconsistent resolution between the two paths.
findings.recommendation: Resolve stored assignment roles through _resolve_role (honoring AUTHZ_ROLE_LOOKUP) too, or validate/normalize body.roles to IDs at assignment time and reject unknown references.

findings.title: No tests cover the role-assignment subset bypass or the bootstrap '*' escalation
findings.scenario: test_direct_subject_grant_is_subset_gated only exercises body.capabilities; no test assigns body.roles pointing at a role whose caps exceed the granter (the authz-002 hole). test_platform_capabilities_are_refused_but_authz_manage_is_allowed only tries the literal 'platform.authz' and never '*' (the authz-001 hole). The two most serious escalation paths are entirely untested, so the suite passes while the holes are open — a 'tests that stop testing' gap.
findings.evidence: @pytest.mark.parametrize("cap", ["platform.authz", "platform.operators", "authz.manage"])
findings.recommendation: Add tests: (a) tenant admin assigning an over-privileged existing role via body.roles must 403; (b) bootstrap with capabilities=['*'] must 400.

findings.title: Admin list routes silently truncate at AUTHZ_LIST_LIMIT with no pagination
findings.scenario: GET /roles and GET /policies call list_roles/list_policies which pass list_limit (AUTHZ_LIST_LIMIT, default 100) and expose no `after` cursor to the caller. A tenant with more than 100 roles/policies has the rest silently dropped from the admin view; an operator auditing 'who can do what' sees an arbitrary subset and may believe a role/policy is absent. (The PDP path correctly pages to exhaustion via all_for; the admin views do not.)
findings.evidence: return {"roles": await build_authz(request).list_roles(_op_tenant(principal))}
findings.recommendation: Expose pagination (after cursor + next token) on the admin list endpoints, or page to exhaustion, so the admin view cannot silently truncate.

findings.title: Bootstrap and erase record actor="" though the internal caller identity is available
findings.scenario: require_internal_token resolves a CallerIdentity (named for static/jwks drivers). But authz.tenant_bootstrapped and subject.erased are recorded with actor="", discarding it. An investigation into 'who bootstrapped this tenant admin' or 'who erased this subject' cannot attribute the action to a caller, weakening the audit trail exactly on privileged internal mutations.
findings.evidence:
await request.app.state.auditor.record(
        "authz.tenant_bootstrapped", actor="", tenant=tenant, resource=f"tenant:{tenant}", ...)
findings.recommendation: Thread the resolved CallerIdentity.caller (from require_internal_token) into the audit actor for internal-tier mutations.

findings.title: ABAC 'in'/'contains' operators do substring matching on strings
findings.scenario: _apply implements 'in' as `left in right` and 'contains' as `right in left`. When the operand is a string rather than a list, Python 'in' is substring containment: a condition {attr:'subject.id', op:'in', value:'$allowed'} with allowed='alice-admin' would match subject.id='admin' or 'ice'. A policy author intending set membership can get unintended matches, potentially granting access to a subject whose id is a substring of an allowed value.
findings.evidence:
if op == "in":
            return left in right if right is not None else False
findings.recommendation: Require the right operand to be a list/tuple/set for 'in'/'nin' (and left for 'contains'); return False for string operands, or add an explicit substring operator distinct from membership.

findings.title: _subject_caps does an N+1 role fetch on the PDP hot path when the cache misses
findings.scenario: On a subject-caps cache miss, _subject_caps issues one self._roles.get(role_id) per assigned role sequentially. For a subject with many roles this is N round-trips to the datastore on the platform's hottest path (an authorization decision runs on effectively every request), amplifying latency on cold cache / after every PAP write bumps the generation.
findings.evidence:
for role_id in a.roles:
            role = await self._roles.get(role_id)
findings.recommendation: Batch-fetch the roles (a single multi-get / IN query) or cache the role->caps map per tenant generation and intersect, avoiding per-role round-trips.

findings.title: Erasure paginates assignments sorted by a non-existent 'created' field
findings.scenario: erase() calls store.find(_ASSIGN, ..., sort=("created", "asc")) but Assignment.to_dict emits no 'created' key (only id/subject/tenant/roles/capabilities). The pagination/sort relies on the store tolerating a missing sort key; on a stricter store (e.g. postgres) this can error or order non-deterministically, and the cursor could skip or repeat rows, leaving an assignment un-erased on a paged DSAR.
findings.evidence: rows, cursor = await self._store.find(_ASSIGN, {"tenant": tenant, "subject": subject}, limit=500, after=cursor, sort=("created", "asc"))
findings.recommendation: Sort by a field that exists on the row (e.g. 'id' or 'subject'), consistent with AssignmentStore.all_for which sorts by 'subject'.

findings.title: CheckIn.subject defaults to empty string, allowing decisions for an empty subject
findings.scenario: CheckIn.subject has default="" and no min_length. A check with an omitted subject resolves the assignment keyed on (tenant, "") and would match any assignment accidentally stored under an empty subject, plus role/extra caps. An empty-subject decision is almost never meaningful and can mask caller bugs (subject silently dropped) as an allow/deny answer.
findings.evidence:
class CheckIn(BaseModel):
    subject: str = Field(default="", max_length=256)
findings.recommendation: Require a non-empty subject for check (min_length=1) unless a pure action/attribute policy check is an intended, documented mode.

findings.title: Policy cache key is not length-prefixed unlike subject/role keys
findings.scenario: _subject_caps and _role_caps deliberately length-prefix the tenant to avoid (tenant,subject)/(tenant,ref) key collisions, but _tenant_policies uses f"authz:pol:{gen}:{tenant}" with no such prefixing. It is lower risk (gen is numeric and tenant is the last segment), but the inconsistency means a future key extension or an unusual tenant/gen encoding could collide two tenants' cached policy sets — a cross-tenant policy leak.
findings.evidence: key = f"authz:pol:{gen}:{tenant}"
findings.recommendation: Length-prefix the tenant here too for consistency with the subject/role cache keys.

findings.title: internal_effective 'roles' input is expanded with no ownership/subset check
findings.scenario: GET /internal/authz/effective expands the caller-supplied comma-separated `roles` into capabilities (the roles the caller claims the subject holds) with no verification that the caller is entitled to assert them. This is intentional trust in identity, but combined with the shared-token driver (caller unnamed) any internal service can mint an inflated capability answer for any subject/tenant, which identity then embeds into a token. Documented as by-design but worth an explicit route-policy restriction to a named caller.
findings.recommendation: Gate this route in INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON to the identity service's named caller (static/jwks driver), so the trust is proven rather than assumed.

findings.title: Combined engine deny-overrides only when an ABAC deny 'matched'; unmatched deny policies never fire against an RBAC allow
findings.scenario: CombinedEngine returns the ABAC decision only when ad.matched_policy is not None and not ad.allow. If a subject holds the capability via RBAC, an ABAC deny that fails to match purely because its condition references an attribute the caller did not supply (so evaluate() returns False) is skipped, and RBAC allow wins. Because ABAC attributes are supplied by the caller (internal_check body.attributes), a caller can suppress a conditional deny by omitting the attribute it keys on, then rely on RBAC to allow.
findings.recommendation: Document that conditional deny policies must not depend on caller-optional attributes for a hard deny, and consider treating a missing required attribute in a deny condition as fail-closed (deny) rather than non-match.

remediation.note: CRITICAL + all 3 HIGH fixed with tests: authz-001 wildcard bootstrap (forbidden_caps rejects */platform.*/plat*), authz-002 role-assignment subset gate, authz-003 gen fail-closed on cache error (bypass, no stale caps), authz-004 backup/import audited (new critical action). MEDIUM/LOW still pending.
